solution.concept_anchor: Stupa classification criteria relic commemorative votive

statement_analysis.statement: Relic stupas (dhatu-chetiya) are classified based on the presence of bodily relics of the Buddha or his principal disciples, while commemorative stupas (udesika-chetiya) mark locations associated with significant events in the Buddha's life.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the standard Theravada classification of stupas: dhatu-chetiya (relic stupas), udesika-chetiya (commemorative stupas), and paribhoga-chetiya (stupas over objects of use) — the distinction described is accurate.

statement_analysis.statement: The Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya is classified as a relic stupa (dhatu-chetiya) because it was built over a portion of the Bodhi tree's root system.
statement_analysis.reason: The Mahabodhi Temple is a commemorative monument (udesika-chetiya) marking the site of the Enlightenment — it is not a relic stupa; no bodily relics are associated with its classification, and its structure is a temple tower (shikhara), not a stupa dome.

statement_analysis.statement: Paribhoga stupas (stupas over objects used by the Buddha) are categorised separately from both relic and commemorative stupas in classical Buddhist architectural classification.
statement_analysis.reason: The Theravada tripartite classification includes paribhoga-chetiya as a distinct third category covering objects of use (bowl, robe, etc.) — separate from bodily relics and commemorative locations.

statement_analysis.statement: Votive stupas, by definition, cannot belong to any of the three canonical stupa categories (relic, commemorative, paribhoga) as they serve a merit-making function outside doctrinal classification.
statement_analysis.reason: Votive stupas can contain secondary relic deposits or replicate the form of a relic stupa for merit-making; the canonical tripartite classification and the votive category are not mutually exclusive — some votive stupas also function as secondary relic stupas.

solution.strong_distractor: c — A student correctly counting Statements 1 and 3 as correct may not carefully examine Statement 4's 'cannot belong by definition' absolute qualifier and will count three correct statements.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — the relic/commemorative distinction using Pali terminology is accurate.
Statement 2 is incorrect — the Mahabodhi Temple is commemorative, not a relic stupa; it is also architecturally a temple tower, not a dome stupa.
Statement 3 is correct — paribhoga-chetiya is a legitimate third category in Theravada classification.
Statement 4 is incorrect — 'cannot by definition' is an unjustified absolute; votive stupas can and do incorporate relic deposits.
Two statements (1 and 3) are correct — the answer is (b) Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 conflates the Bodhi tree's sanctity with the concept of bodily relics. Students who know Bodh Gaya is the most sacred Buddhist site will assume it must be a relic stupa, not recognising that the doctrinal category of 'relic' (dhatu) refers specifically to bodily remains, not sacred trees or locations.
solution.final_explanation:
Buddhist stupa classification according to Theravada doctrine follows a tripartite system based on what the stupa enshrines or commemorates.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Dhatu-chetiya (bodily relics) and udesika-chetiya (commemorative locations) are two of the three canonical stupa categories — accurately described.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya is an udesika-chetiya (commemorative) — it marks the site of the Enlightenment, not a relic deposit. The structure is architecturally a shikhara tower, not a hemispherical stupa.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Paribhoga-chetiya (stupas enshrining objects used by the Buddha — his bowl, robe, begging bowl, etc.) is the third canonical category, distinct from the other two.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: The 'cannot by definition' claim is an unsupported absolute; votive stupas are a functional category (merit-making), not a doctrinal one, and can overlap with relic or commemorative categories.

Two statements correct → (b) Only two.

Value Addition:
• The Theravada tripartite classification (dhatu, paribhoga, udesika) is described in the Milindapanha and other Pali texts.
• The Ruwanwelisaya stupa in Sri Lanka is a classic example of a dhatu-chetiya claiming relics of the Buddha.
• The Mahabodhi Temple received UNESCO World Heritage status in 2002 — separate from Sanchi (1989).

solution.concept_anchor: Sanchi torana structural components
solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who associate torana with 'three architraves' (a memorable feature) may select (d) thinking all toranas at Sanchi have two uprights and two lintels; the actual number of architraves is three, but this option conflates correct and incorrect numbers.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): a torana does not have four uprights — two uprights (posts) is the standard form.
Eliminate (c): two architraves is incorrect for Sanchi toranas — the characteristic feature is three superimposed horizontal architraves.
Eliminate (d): 'four uprights and two architraves' combines a wrong upright count with a wrong architrave count.

Select (b): each Sanchi torana consists of two square posts (uprights) and three horizontal projecting architraves — the three-architrave arrangement is among the most distinctive structural features of these gateways.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap is the number of architraves. Students know that Sanchi toranas have 'horizontal beams' but have not memorised the specific count of three. Options (c) and (d) are crafted to exploit this uncertainty by offering the plausible-but-wrong count of two.
solution.final_explanation:
The structural form of the Sanchi toranas is architecturally precise and frequently tested.

• Option (a) — Four uprights and three horizontal projecting beams: Incorrect. There are two uprights (square posts), not four, at each torana.
• Option (b) — Two square posts and three superimposed projecting architraves: Correct. Each Sanchi torana consists of two massive square stone posts and three horizontal projecting beams (architraves) stacked one above the other, with sculpted panels on all surfaces.
• Option (c) — Two uprights and two horizontal architraves: Incorrect. The number of architraves is three, not two — a commonly misremembered detail.
• Option (d) — Four uprights and two architraves: Incorrect. Both numbers are wrong.

Value Addition:
• The three horizontal architraves at Sanchi toranas project on both sides of the uprights, creating a distinctive horizontal emphasis that has been compared to wooden gateway prototypes.
• The sculpted narrative panels fill the spaces between and around the architraves — including the volute spirals at the ends, often featuring elephants, yakshis, and lotuses.
• Each architrave terminates in a large spiral volute — one of the most recognisable motifs in Sanchi art.
